_comment: Optimizely.Performance.Counters - settings template for CMS 12 and CMS 13.
Merge the 'Optimizely' block below into your site's appsettings.json. Every value shown is
the default, so a site that copies this file wholesale behaves exactly as it does with no
configuration at all - delete the lines you are not changing.
Keys beginning with an underscore are comments and are ignored. Anything else the package
does not recognise is logged as a warning at startup, so a typo is visible rather than silent.
This is a different section from Optimizely:PerformanceCounters, which belongs to
Optimizely.Performance.DotNetCounters. The two packages are usually installed together and
configured separately.

_comment_Enabled: The master switch. False and nothing is decorated, no probe starts and no counter is
registered with Application Insights - the modules log one line each and return. It is
here so that an operator suspecting this package during an incident can rule it out with
a setting rather than a deployment.

_comment: The four probes measure conditions nothing publishes a counter for. Each can be turned
off on its own. GarbageCollection and Contention need .NET 6 or later and never run on
CMS 11 whatever they are set to; CacheLock finds nothing on CMS 11 for the same reason
the cascade counters are absent there.

ThreadPool._comment_SampleIntervalSeconds: Each sample is one queued work item.
ThreadPool._comment_SampleTimeoutSeconds: A sample that does not finish inside this is recorded as starvation.
ThreadPool._comment_SlowSampleThresholdMilliseconds: Delay above which a sample is also logged.

GarbageCollection._comment_SlowPauseThresholdMilliseconds: Pause above which a sample is also logged.

_comment_BurstCaptureEnabled: False leaves the contention rate running and stops the short capture bursts that
measure how long the waits were. The rate is the free half of the probe.
_comment_BurstTriggerContentionsPerSecon: Contention is normal and a busy site produces a steady background rate. The default
sits well above it, so a burst means something changed.

_comment_Enabled: The switch for the only reflection over Optimizely internals in the package. False
loses the four Optimizely.CMS.Cache.Lock* counters and nothing else.
CacheLock._comment_QueueDepthThreshold: Total queue depth above which a sample is logged. Zero silences the log.

_comment_Enabled: False leaves IMemoryCache undecorated, which removes the cost as well as the nine
cascade counters. Cache hit, miss and invalidation rates are measured a layer up and
are unaffected. Has no effect on CMS 11, which has no IMemoryCache under its object
_comment_LargeRemovalThreshold: A counter cannot carry a cache key, so a cascade this size or larger is also written
to the log, naming the key responsible. That is the only way to find out which key is
Cascade._comment_FailureThreshold: Consecutive failures after which the recorder switches itself off for the process.

_comment: The log write rate counters. Not under Probes, because this is not a probe: a probe
looks on its own thread, and this counts on whichever thread wrote the log entry.
On CMS 12 and CMS 13 the counting is done by an ILoggerProvider named
OptimizelyLogWriteRate, which sees every write the host's logging dispatches. It counts
at the host's default minimum level; to widen what it sees without changing what any
real sink writes, set Logging:OptimizelyLogWriteRate:LogLevel:Default in the standard
ASP.NET Core logging section. On CMS 11 the same counters come from a log4net appender
instead and this switch controls both.
False loses the three Optimizely.Runtime.Logging.* counters and nothing else. The
provider is then not registered at all, so it costs the site nothing.
Outbound response cacheability. Every response the site sends is classified from its
Cache-Control and Expires headers as the headers go out, and the nine
Optimizely.Runtime.Http.* counters report the mix once a minute: what share of responses
is shared-cacheable, browser-only, revalidating, no-store, or says nothing at all.
The one thing here that is not a number is the shared-cache conflict: a response marked
public that also sets a cookie. No shared cache will store it, so the cache headers on
that route are buying nothing - and from the origin's side the traffic that results
looks like ordinary traffic.
Not under Probes, for the same reason Logging is not: nothing goes looking. The counting
happens on the thread that is about to write the response, and costs a header read and
two or three interlocked increments.
On CMS 12 and CMS 13 the measurement is middleware, registered first in the pipeline so
that it sees the finished header set; on CMS 11 it is an HTTP module that the package
adds to the pipeline itself, so there is nothing to put in web.config. Integrated mode
only - classic mode has no managed response header collection to read.
_comment_LogSharedCacheConflicts: A counter cannot carry a route, so a conflicting response is also written to the log,
naming the path that produced it. That is the only way to find the code responsible.
The path is logged without its query string, deliberately. False keeps the counter and
stops the log line, which is what a site that knows about the conflict wants.
_comment_SharedCacheConflictLogsPerMinut: One misconfigured route serving steadily would otherwise write the same sentence on
every request. Zero silences the log as completely as the switch above.
Http._comment_FailureThreshold: Consecutive failures after which the recorder switches itself off for the process.

_comment: The only switch in this file that is not about a measurement. Everything else decides
whether a counter is produced; this decides how the counters that are produced leave
the process.
Every counter is published twice: to the Optimizely-Performance EventSource, and to a
System.Diagnostics.Metrics meter of the same name carrying the same counter names. The
meter is the only path that reaches OpenTelemetry, UseAzureMonitor() or Application
Insights SDK 3.x - none of which collect EventCounters at all, because the
EventCounterCollector package stopped at 2.23.0 and has no 3.x. Subscribe with one line:
.WithMetrics(m => m.AddMeter("Optimizely-Performance"))
Defaults to true because the failure it prevents is silent: with the meter off, a site
on any of those hosts publishes every counter to nobody and nothing says so. Leaving it
on where nothing collects meters costs a call that returns on a disabled instrument.
Ignored on CMS 11, which has no System.Diagnostics.Metrics. The setting is left here so
one settings file serves all three majors.
The only node in this file that is not about a counter. Everything else measures the
running site; this records what was deployed, so a change in one can be attributed to
a change in the other.
At startup and on a heartbeat the bin folder is scanned and reduced to a 16-character
fingerprint over every assembly's identity - its MVID, the compiler's own id for the
exact bits, so a rebuild of the same version reads as a change and a version bump
without a rebuild does not. Four events go to Application Insights under names starting
OptiCounters., and the fingerprint is also stamped onto every request, dependency and
exception the site sends as a DeploymentFingerprint custom dimension. Grouping any chart
by that dimension is what makes 'did the release cause this' a query rather than an
argument about timestamps.
False emits nothing, stamps nothing and does not scan.
_comment_StatePath: Where the last manifest is kept, so the next start can diff against it. Empty means
probe for somewhere writable in order - App Service's /home/data, then ProgramData,
then the temporary directory - and report on every event which one won and whether it
Worth setting only if you have somewhere that genuinely outlives a deployment, such as
a mounted share. On DXP the container is replaced wholesale on every release, so no
path inside it is durable and every start reports as a baseline rather than a diff -
which is why the manifest event carries the fingerprint on every row. The comparison
happens in the query instead, and needs no state at all.
_comment_InventoryMode: When the one-row-per-assembly listing is emitted. OnChange sends it once per process
start, again whenever the fingerprint changes, and again every InventoryReemitHours so
the answer never ages out of retention. Always adds every heartbeat, which is the same
few hundred rows over and over - useful while proving the feature out, expensive as a
standing setting. Never keeps the manifest and the change events and drops the listing,
which loses the ability to answer what a given fingerprint actually contained.
_comment_HeartbeatMinutes: How often the bin folder is rescanned. This is also how quickly an out-of-band change -
a hotfixed DLL copied onto one instance - is noticed, and how long after a rolling
deployment the fleet is confirmed to have converged.
_comment_IncludeSystemAssemblies: False drops System.* and Microsoft.* from the scan, which makes the inventory shorter
and the fingerprint blind to a runtime patch. Whatever this is set to, set it the same
on every instance: two instances scanning to different rules report as diverged.
_comment_IncludeFilePaths: False by default. The file name and version identify an assembly; the full path adds
the host's directory layout to telemetry that is otherwise about the deployment.
_comment_StampTelemetry: The DeploymentFingerprint dimension on every telemetry item. False keeps the events and
loses the join - the events would then say what changed and when, and nothing would
connect that to a request. application_Version is left to the host either way.
_comment_MaxChangeEvents: A cap on the per-assembly change rows one transition can emit. A first start on a host
with no durable state is a baseline and emits none; a genuine framework upgrade can
change hundreds. Hitting the cap is written to the log.
Deployment._comment_MaxAssemblies: A cap on the scan itself. A truncated scan says so on the manifest event.
